source: Every figure is the 'everything outstanding' line of the matching ownership book on this tab (Federal Reserve Financial Accounts, Bank of Japan Flow of Funds, ONS UK Economic Accounts, ECB and Eurostat quarterly sector accounts, Statistics Canada National Balance Sheet Accounts, Central Bank of the Republic of China Flow of Funds, India's exchange shareholding filings, and the OECD financial balance sheets for the economies outside the euro area whose owners are known only as residents and foreigners), converted with the International Monetary Fund's end-of-period exchange rates.
note: Each line is one pool of financial wealth whose owners the tab can already name, shown at what the whole pool is worth rather than at any one owner's share, so adding the lines gives the wealth this tab can account for. For some markets the owners are known by kind, such as households, funds, banks and foreigners; for others only as residents against foreigners, and those lines say so, with a subtotal for each tier so it is clear how much rests on the coarser split. Each pool counts what its own residents issued, so a Japanese share owned by an American fund is counted once, in Japan's pool, where Americans are among the foreign owners; the Federal Reserve's American figures for company shares, corporate bonds and some loans also include such holdings, and the ledger takes that part out and shows how much. In the same way the euro-area line already includes every member country, so no member has a line of its own, and international bonds are left out because they already sit inside each country's own bond figures. Money and bank credit are not added in, because a deposit is the same money as the loan that created it; they have their own charts. A country's figure is carried forward for up to a year while its next release is awaited, and any market whose newest figure is older than that drops out of the total rather than repeating a stale number. Fund shares are kept in, as the holder-as-filed view counts them, and their line says how much of the total they are, since a fund's shares are worth the securities it holds and those securities are counted here too. This is not the whole world: the pools we know are missing, and why, are listed in the table under this chart. Technical detail: amounts are each market's own published total outstanding, or for the OECD economies the total issued by residents, converted at the International Monetary Fund's end-of-period rate for that quarter, with euro amounts converted only from 1999 and any rate more than a year old refused.
